catalog_quote: 1.4 Stress and length. Word stress is phonemic, occurring on the penultimate or ultimate syllable of a word. The following words are minimal stress pairs: /híku/ 'elbow' /hikú/ 'I'; /púsuq/ 'banana blossom' /pusúq/ 'heart'; /maŋálih/ 'to dig' /maŋalíh/ 'to remove'. When a word base is suffixed, most notably with /-ɨn/ or /-an/, the stress typically shifts to the right one syllable: /gámit/ + /-ɨn/ → /gamítɨn/ 'to use'; /halíw/ + /-ɨn/ → /haliwɨ́n/ 'to buy'; /tápun/ + /-an/ → /tapúnan/ 'to throw'; /tambáy/ + /-an/ → /tambayán/ 'to help'. Vowel length occurs independently of stress and is phonemic. The following words are minimal length pairs: /manurúq/ 'to teach' /ma:nurúq/ 'teacher'; /maŋiturúq/ 'to point' /ma:ŋiturúq/ 'one who points'; /tapúnan/ 'to throw' /ta:púnan/ 'to throw to each other'.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the catalog's own source: the catalog record for boto1242 (classification lexical, the primary-stress rule 'Word stress is phonemic.. penultimate or ultimate syllable.. unpredictably', deciding quote identical to sec. 1.4) was built from this Rosetta excerpt and re-verified. The page scan read today confirms the quote verbatim (the scanned text has garbles such as '|«Akultimate' for 'penultimate'; the image is the record). Nothing new beyond the orthography remark that stress and length are not usually.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically contrastive and confined to the last two syllables: any word has stress on either the penult or the ultima, and which one is not predictable from the form (minimal pairs). When a suffix (-ɨn, -an) is added the stress moves one syllable to the right, so it keeps its distance from the word end. Vowel length is a separate phonemic feature, independent of stress. The practical orthography does not mark stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts one syllable rightward under suffixation with /-ɨn/ or /-an/ ('typically'); no other exceptions stated. Loanwords with consonant clusters are mentioned in 1.3 but nothing is said about their stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Antworth 1979 describes Botolan Sambal (Sambal of Botolan, Zambales) = boto1242, the catalog language. The listed Reid 1971 archive.org item (rosettaproject_ilk_phon-1) actually describes Ilongot, Kakiduge:n dialect (Bugkalut; ISO ilk), a different language, and is not evidence for Sambal. The Stone 2006 ICAL Sambalic paper already held by the project contains no mention of stress or accent.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Botolan Sambal has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this dictionary adds lexical evidence (stress-marked headwords, a stress minimal pair, an explicit 'stress difference' note) that stress is contrastive and falls on the penult or the final syllable per lexeme. It contains no rule statement to agree or disagree with. This is consistent with the Antworth 1979 sketch excerpt already held by the project from an earlier reading (sec. 1.4: word stress phonemic, on the penultimate or ultimate syllable).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The dictionary gives no prose statement about stress at all (no introduction, orthography note or appendix; the disk copy was checked from the handwritten title page through p. 473). Every headword is typed with an accent diacritic on one vowel, on varying syllables (final in abaká, abalayán, abantí, abáng, talín; penult in abakáda, abágat, ábang, ábaw, ábay, abáya, talíno), and the compilers treat its position as contrastive: ábang 'rent' vs abáng 'ambush' is a minimal pair on p. 1, and under tálip (p. 408) the two senses of the paNG- derivative ('knife' vs 'peeling') are said to differ by a 'stress difference'. Read as lexically specified stress (penult or final), not predictable by rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing (no prose; only one accent mark per headword in the pages inspected, though some entries such as abálà and talindátà carry a second diacritic on the final vowel, which may mark a final glottal/grave rather than stress; the document does not explain its diacritics)
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; p. 408 note implies derivational stress alternation in paNG- + tálip
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary is of Botolan Sambal (title page 'Dictionary of Botolan Sambal, August, 1968'); a few headwords are tagged (E) or (sp..) as English/Spanish loans. No dialect subdivision is indicated.

tone_statements.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1993. Overview of Austronesian and Philippine accent patterns. In Jerold A. Edmondson & Kenneth J. Gregerson (eds.), Tonality in Austronesian Languages (Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 24), 17-24. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press. [paper read at 6ICAL, Honolulu, 22 May 1991]
tone_statements.quote: Both word accent and intonation involve three details: 1) long vs short vowels (length), 2) pitch or high vs low tones (pitch accent), 3) loudness or amplitude (stress). … In Philippine languages, vowel iength (or shortness) is the most important feature of word accent … In all Philippine languages stress or pitch accent is a syntactic (grammatical) feature, a means of indicating an accent group (phrase); it does not even necessarily coincide with length. … (A) Phonemic length and shortness, as inherited from PPH (< PHN, PMP, PAN): … Malaweg, Sambal, Tagalog.
tone_statements.locator: p. 18 (sec. 2), p. 19 (sec. 3 opening) and p. 20 (sec. 6, Table 2, class A)
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone: Philippine-type contrastive word accent realised chiefly as vowel length with pitch and stress as secondary correlates; Sambal classed with Tagalog/Ilokano as retaining Proto-Philippine phonemic length (class A).

sources.citation: Houck, Charlotte and Harriet Minot (comps.). 1966. Expanded Philippine Word List -- 1966. Language: Aeta (Negrito); Location: Botolan, Zambales; June 1966. Typescript, 12 pp.: 372-item wordlist, pronoun and demonstrative paradigms, and a two-page appendix 'Phonemes of Aeta' (pp. 10-11, 'taken from an unpublished data paper with addenda by Harriet Minot, S.I.L.'). SIL Philippines; SIL Language & Culture Archives item 80795 ('Sambal - Botolan wordlist (1966)').
sources.note: The 'Phonemes of Aeta' appendix gives an exhaustive phoneme inventory (16 consonants p t k b d g m n ng l r s h ʔ w y; 4 vowels a e[pepet] i o), allophony, syllable patterns and word shapes, and closes with the only suprasegmental statement: stress is phonemic, contrastive on the penult or ultima, with rhythmic secondary stresses on every second or every third preceding syllable ('not yet thoroughly analyzed'). Tone, pitch and intonation are not mentioned anywhere; no tonal contrast is posited. (Vowel length, which Antworth 1979 treats as phonemic, is not mentioned either.).

tone.quote: Phonemes of Aeta: (This material is taken from an unpublished data paper with addenda by Harriet Minot, S.I.L. [...] The analysis was made on the basis of the syllable.) The phonemes of Aeta are as follows: b,k,d,g,h,l,m,n,ng,p,r,s,t,ʔ,y,w,a,e,i, and o. [...] [p. 11:] Stress is a phonemic feature, occurring contrastively on the penult or ultima. It also occurs on other syllables preceding these in two patterns: either every other syllable is stressed or every third syllable is stressed. This phase is not yet thoroughly analyzed.
